parts.title: Three weeks at the windmill
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last summer, I spent three weeks helping to repair an old windmill near my grandmother's village. I had never done anything like it before. The windmill is almost three hundred years old, and for fifty years it stood empty, until a local group decided to save it.

On the first morning, a woman called Jean gave us hard hats and boots and showed us around. The building was dirtier than I had expected, and there were birds' nests in every corner. Our first job was to clean the floor, which took the whole day. I was tired and a little bored, and I wondered why I had come.

Then Jean showed us the old machinery. The heavy stones that once turned the grain into flour were still there. When she explained how they worked, I suddenly understood how much effort had been needed to make a single loaf of bread. After that, I looked at everything differently.

By the end of the three weeks, we had painted the doors, repaired the stairs and put new glass in two windows. The windmill is not working yet, but next spring visitors will be able to walk through it. I plan to go back and take my grandmother with me, because she remembers the mill from when she was a girl.

questions.prompt: What happened to the windmill before the group saved it?
options: Nobody used it for fifty years
It was a farm shop for a while
It was closed because it was unsafe
questions.explanation: The text says it stood empty for fifty years.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel on the first day?
questions.explanation: He says he was tired and a little bored, and wondered why he had come.

questions.prompt: What changed the way he felt about the work?
questions.explanation: After Jean explained the stones, he understood how much effort bread took and looked at everything differently.

questions.prompt: What did the volunteers do during the three weeks?
options: Make flour for the first visitors
Build a new roof for the windmill
Repair and paint parts of the building
questions.explanation: They painted the doors, repaired the stairs and put glass in two windows.

questions.prompt: Why does he want to take his grandmother to the windmill?
options: She has never seen a windmill
She wants to help with the painting
She knew it when she was young
questions.explanation: His grandmother remembers the mill from when she was a girl.

parts.title: The old bridge at Oakham
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
The Old Bridge in Oakham is only four metres wide, and cars have not been allowed on it since 1975. [1] Every day, hundreds of walkers and cyclists use it to get to the market on the other side.

The bridge was built in 1420 by local monks, who needed a safe way to carry their goods across the river. [2] It is said that the builders mixed eggs into the mortar, which made the stones stronger. Scientists tested this idea last year, and they found that it was probably true.

In 1968, the town council wanted to knock the bridge down and build a wider one. [3] Thousands of people signed a letter, and a newspaper wrote about the plan. In the end, the council changed its mind.

Today, the bridge is looked after by a group of volunteers. [4] They also pull rubbish out of the water every spring. At the end of the bridge, a small sign tells the story of its history in three languages. [5] Visitors often stop to read it and take photographs before they cross.
sentences: Every month, they check the stones and repair any that have become loose.
The river itself is one of the cleanest in the country.
Local people were angry and decided to fight the plan.
Instead, it has become one of the most popular walks in the area.
The words were written by pupils from the local school.
Before then, people had to cross the river in a small boat, which was often dangerous.

gaps.explanation: The sentence says what the bridge is now, and the next sentence says that hundreds of walkers and cyclists use it.
The sentence explains the need for a bridge, because the monks wanted a safe way to cross and the next sentence tells how it was built.
The sentence shows how people reacted to the plan, and then thousands signed a letter.
The sentence describes the volunteers' regular work, and "They also" adds another job.
The sentence says who wrote the words on the sign, which visitors then stop to read.

parts.title: Welcome to the heritage weekend
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: mattias
turns.text: Good morning, and welcome to the Heritage Weekend in Stanton. My name is Mattias, and I'm the organiser. The weekend begins today at nine and ends on Sunday at six. About thirty old buildings in the town are open to the public, and all of them are free. You can pick up a map from the information tent in the main square. If you like churches, don't miss St Anne's, where there is a concert of old music at three o'clock. The old school is showing photographs from 1920. The train station has a small museum for children, and they can try on old uniforms. Buses between the buildings are free and leave every twenty minutes. If you would like lunch, there's a restaurant in the town hall that serves traditional soup, but you should reserve a table, because it fills quickly. Finally, please remember to take your rubbish with you. Enjoy the weekend!

parts.title: An archaeologist at work
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: harlan
turns.text: Today I'm talking to Margit Olsen, an archaeologist. Margit, what made you choose this job?

turns.speaker: margit
turns.text: When I was ten, I found an old pot while playing on a beach with my father. A teacher at the museum told me that it was nearly two thousand years old, and from that day I wanted to find more.

turns.speaker: harlan
turns.text: What's a normal day like on a dig?

turns.speaker: margit
turns.text: We start at seven, because it gets very hot later. Most of the day I'm on my knees with a small brush, moving the soil away very slowly. It sounds boring, but I find it relaxing.

turns.speaker: harlan
turns.text: What's the most exciting thing you've found?

turns.speaker: margit
turns.text: A child's toy, a little horse made of clay. Somebody lost it almost three thousand years ago, and I was the first person to touch it since then.

turns.speaker: harlan
turns.text: Is the job dangerous?

turns.speaker: margit
turns.text: Not really. The worst problems are sunburn and insects. Once I fell into a hole, but I only hurt my pride.

turns.speaker: harlan
turns.text: What happens to the things you find?

turns.speaker: margit
turns.text: Most go to the local museum, but first we clean them, measure them and take photographs. That can take months.

turns.speaker: harlan
turns.text: What would you say to someone who wants to do this work?

turns.speaker: margit
turns.text: Study hard, but also join a local dig as a volunteer. You'll learn a great deal in two weeks in the field.
